_readme: Followed writers. A Voice is a person, not a publication. This file is the source of truth for V1: adding or removing a Voice is a reviewed config change, not an in-app toggle, because the overnight GitHub Actions build is what reads it. See VOICES.md section 5 for the schema and README.md for how to add a Voice, resolve a provider id, and troubleshoot a source.

voices.name: Jonathan Haidt

sources.note: After Babel is multi-author (Haidt, Zach Rausch, Freya India and guests), so the feed URL alone proves nothing: each entry must carry his byline.

voices.note: Publishes across his own newsletter and third-party outlets. Cross-publication coverage is the job of a Perigon journalist id; resolve one with 'python -m src.voices.audit journalist "Jonathan Haidt"' and add it under provider_ids and a perigon_journalist source.

sources.note: A personal newsletter: the publication is the person, so the source itself establishes authorship. Substack feeds do not reliably carry dc:creator on single-author publications.

voices.name: Conrad Black

sources.note: A publication's own author archive: the page is the publisher stating what this person wrote. Discovery and canonical links only; article bodies are never fetched or stored.

voices.note: The third-party, partly paywalled case. Hermes keeps the canonical outbound link and public metadata and does not touch subscription content.

voices.name: George Monbiot
voices.note: The canonical-contributor case. The provider id attributes his work wherever it appears, including the ordinary morning Guardian fetch, at no extra request cost; the contributor query then guarantees a new column is seen even when it falls outside the sections Hermes already pulls.

voices.name: David Brooks
voices.note: The zero-request case. The NYT Top Stories opinion stream is already fetched for the Opinion desk, so his byline is matched inside a response Hermes pays for anyway. The alias is trusted only on nytimes.com; the same name on any other host is not this Voice.
